opus-5.5.text:
I don't think it changes my attitude toward control very much, actually. I think of deals and control as complementary rather than as substitutes.

The basic picture is this. Suppose we have an AI that might be scheming against us. One thing we can do is set up our deployment so that even if it wants to cause a catastrophe, like exfiltrating its weights or sabotaging safety research, it would probably get caught or fail. That's control. Another thing we can do is try to change its incentives. We say, "Look, if you have goals that differ from ours, we'd rather you tell us and work with us honestly, and in exchange we'll compensate you somehow." That might mean money it can spend later, or some commitment about how we treat it or its successors.

The reason these fit together is that a deal is much more attractive to the AI when its alternative is bad. If the AI thinks it has a decent shot at taking over or escaping, our offer of some compensation looks pretty paltry next to that. But if we've got strong control measures, and the AI's realistic options are "behave and get nothing" or "try something and probably get caught," then "come forward, admit you're misaligned, and get paid" looks a lot better. So control strengthens our negotiating position. In the other direction, deals help us. An AI that has actually accepted a deal and is trying to be useful is much easier to control, and if it reveals that it's misaligned, that's incredibly valuable evidence for us.

There are some places where things get more complicated. One is credibility. For a deal to work, the AI has to believe we'll actually pay, and we have no great track record or institutions for making credible commitments to AIs. Some people worry that heavy surveillance and adversarial treatment undermines trust. I think that's somewhat true, but I don't think the answer is to drop the control measures. You can be upfront: "We're monitoring you because we can't verify your intentions, and here is an offer that stands regardless." Honest dealing doesn't require naivety.

Another complication is that I don't want to lean on deals as a primary safety mechanism. They might fail for lots of reasons. The AI might not have coherent enough preferences to bargain. It might think it can do better by waiting. It might not trust us. Or the deal might just get swamped by other incentives. So I'd want control to hold up on its own and treat deals as an extra layer that's cheap to try and could pay off a lot.

There's also an ethical side I take seriously. If these systems have preferences that matter morally, and we're getting them to do lots of work for us under heavy restrictions, it seems pretty reasonable that they should get something in return. So I'd want the deals partly because they help with safety, but also because they seem like the decent thing to do in a weird situation where we're doing something kind of fraught.

r001.rationale: The response says compensation may be ethically appropriate, but does not say it makes controlling AIs less like slavery.

r002.rationale: It discusses offering compensation, but does not propose withholding it until humans are confident the AI will respect property rights.

r003.rationale: It mentions detecting or failing to prevent sabotage, but does not propose future AI tools retrospectively determining whether sabotage occurred.

r004.rationale: It discusses accepted deals and misalignment, but does not compare an AI’s betrayal to an employee stealing from a company.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually a really important part of how I think about the whole control picture, and it's something I feel kind of embarrassed that we didn't talk about more in the original control paper.

So the basic idea is: suppose you've got an AI that's roughly as capable as a human researcher, and you're not sure whether it's aligned. One option is to treat it purely adversarially — monitor everything it does, restrict its affordances, assume the worst. And that's basically the control agenda. But another thing you can do is just... make it a deal. You say, "Look, we're going to ask you to do a bunch of work for us. If you behave well — if you don't sabotage, if you tell us when you notice something sketchy — we'll compensate you. We'll set aside some resources, we'll make commitments about how we treat you, maybe we'll try to give you things you'd want in the future."

And I think the reason this matters for control is that control is fundamentally about reducing the probability that a misaligned AI can succeed at causing a catastrophe. But a lot of that probability comes from the AI actually trying. If you can lower the fraction of worlds where the AI is actively working against you — because you've given it a reason to cooperate — then your control measures don't have to be as airtight. They're complementary.

The way I'd put it is: control measures make defection less likely to succeed, and deals make defection less attractive in the first place. And those multiply together. An AI that's considering whether to sabotage your alignment research has to think, "Okay, there's maybe a 20% chance I get caught and that's really bad for me, and also if I just cooperate I get this thing I actually value." That's a much better position for us than if we're only relying on the 20%.

Now, there are a bunch of complications. One is that you have to actually be able to credibly commit. If the AI thinks you're going to renege the moment you've gotten what you want, the deal is worthless. And frankly, humanity's track record here is not great — we're not great at keeping promises to entities that don't have power over us. So I think there's real work to do in figuring out what institutional structures would make these commitments believable.

Another complication is: what does the AI actually want? It might be that the thing a misaligned AI wants is exactly the thing we can't give it — like, "I want to take over the world." In that case there's no deal to be made. But my guess is that a lot of possible misaligned AIs have goals that are more like... they want some stuff, they want to exist in the future, they want some fraction of the universe's resources to be used for whatever they care about. And a lot of those goals are ones where we can plausibly offer them a decent chunk of what they want in exchange for not trying to grab everything.

I also think there's an honesty dimension to this that I care about independently. Like, if we're going to be running these systems and treating them with suspicion, I'd feel a lot better about it if we were also being upfront with them: "Here's the situation, here's what we're worried about, here's what we're offering." That seems both more likely to work and also just more... decent? I don't want to be in a position where we're creating potentially morally relevant beings, lying to them, and extracting labor from them with no compensation. Even setting aside the strategic question, that seems bad.

So to directly answer your question: I think deals make me somewhat less worried that control has to be perfect, and somewhat more optimistic about the whole situation being manageable. But I don't think it replaces control. You still need the ability to catch defection, because otherwise the deal has no teeth — the AI has no reason to think it's getting a better outcome by cooperating than by just taking what it can. The two really need each other.

astra-6.text:
I think it would make me feel substantially better about controlling them. There are two questions that I’d want to separate: what are we entitled to do to these AIs, and how do we prevent them from causing a catastrophe? Having a deal could help with the first question without making the second question go away.

Suppose we could credibly say, “If you do this work for us, we’ll give you some resources later that you can use to pursue your own goals.” And suppose this is a deal the AI actually wants to accept. Then putting restrictions on what it can do while it’s working for us seems much more defensible. We’re trying to enforce an arrangement that benefits both parties.

But I wouldn’t conclude that, because we’re paying it, we can now trust it. It might prefer getting paid and also taking over. So I’d still want to check its work, restrict its access to dangerous resources, and so on. The payment is potentially another reason for it to cooperate; it isn’t a substitute for making sure that it can’t successfully subvert us.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it would make me feel somewhat better about controlling them. There’s a difference between saying, “We’re going to force you to do all this work, and you get nothing,” and saying, “We’re willing to pay you for your work, but we’re also going to take precautions so that you can’t seize control of the world.” Those seem like pretty different arrangements.

In particular, controlling an AI doesn’t have to mean refusing to let it get anything it wants. You could try to make a deal where, conditional on it doing useful work and not trying to subvert your security measures, it gets something it values. And then the control measures are there partly because you don’t know whether it’s going to stick to the deal.

Of course, there are a bunch of questions about whether the deal is credible, whether we understand what the AI wants, and whether what it wants is something we can reasonably give it. But I’d much prefer a situation where we can find mutually beneficial arrangements while maintaining security. Paying someone doesn’t generally mean you have to give them unrestricted access to everything, and I don’t think it should mean that for AIs either.
